senses.definition: To develop a capability by doing the thing repeatedly, on the view that it grows with practice rather than being something a team either has or lacks. The phrase promises reps, not a training course.
senses.caution: It says the ability is missing today. Said about another team that is a criticism in gym clothes; said about your own it is an admission, which is fine only if the next sentence names the actual reps. To a team already at capacity it lands as more work with no more people. It is also coaching-deck language, so in a written board paper it reads as a slogan and invites the obvious question of what the exercise is and who is doing it.
senses.example: We can buy the first three evaluations in. If we want this capability in-house, at some point we have to build that muscle ourselves.

cues.text: Your team keeps handing evaluation work to a consultancy, and you want to argue for doing it in-house repeatedly until they are good at it.
A director asks why you are giving juniors the client presentations when a senior would do a better job today, and your answer is about where the team is in a year.
A friend says they are simply hopeless at cooking, and you want to say the ability is not fixed and comes from doing it over and over.
You have started running twice a week and are explaining to a sceptical relative why the first month feeling awful is the whole point.

distractors: To hire in people who already have the skill, on the view that buying a capability is always faster than growing one.
To write a process down in enough detail that anyone can follow it without asking, so the work stops depending on which particular person happens to be available.
To defend a budget line through a planning round so that a capability survives the cuts. It is a fight about money and about who has the sponsor's attention, and it is usually won before the meeting.

To add headcount to a team that is under pressure, on the assumption that what is short is hands rather than know-how. It is the most common answer to a delivery problem and often the one that makes the next quarter worse, because the new people need teaching.

To keep a capability in-house rather than hand it to a vendor, on the argument that anything genuinely core to the business should not be rented from someone else. The debate is about ownership and long-run dependency, and it tends to get settled on cost rather than on principle.
